links.comparator_used: Discrimination (AUROC) across groups, with no calibration assessment (no formal head-to-head comparison)
links.outcome: Detection of subgroup bias in model performance
links.effect: Calibration differed by race-ethnicity and HPI: predicted hospitalization probabilities were significantly lower for African Americans (0.129±0.051, p=0.016), Hispanics (0.133±0.047, p=0.004), AAPI (0.120±0.051, p=0.018), multi-race (0.245±0.087, p=0.005), and low-HPI areas (0-25%: 0.178±0.042, p<0.001). For hospitalizations, AUROC was similar across races (e.g., 0.781 white, 0.792 Black, 0.757 Hispanic) and across HPI quartiles (0.765-0.780).
links.tradeoff: Evaluation was described as feasible with a part-time statistical analyst. The model was trained on a balanced dataset, so predicted probabilities were far above observed rates. Differential calibration was not detected by gender.
links.quote: There was evidence of differential calibration by race-ethnicity for both ED visits and hospitalizations.

links.comparator_used: Aggregate performance across all patients (implicit; no aggregate-only arm was compared)
links.outcome: Subgroup differences in sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV at the deployed threshold of 60
links.effect: ED visit sensitivity: White 0.495, Black 0.599, Hispanic 0.402, Other 0.381. Hospitalization sensitivity: White 0.392, Black 0.511, AAPI 0.300, Other 0.282. Sensitivity was also higher in the lowest HPI quartile (hospitalization 0.462 vs 0.271 in the highest).
links.tradeoff: Small groups (e.g., AIAN) gave wide confidence intervals and unstable estimates. The operations team kept the 60% outreach threshold to balance reduced bias for some groups against outreach staff bandwidth.
links.quote: Test sensitivity for a decision threshold of 60 also varied among race/ethnicity group with sensitivity lowest among Hispanic and the Other race group and highest among African Americans (Table 3 ).

design_hint: disaggregated calibration and equity audit before/during deployment
